analytic.title: Semi-Federated Scheduling of Mixed-Criticality System for Sporadic DAG Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: DAG task model is a general parallel task model that has been widely concerned and studied by researchers. The combination of mixed-criticality and DAG task model makes it difficult to analyze system behaviors. Under federated mixedcriticality scheduling algorithm, tasks are physically isolated with regard to computation resources, which leads to lower analysis complexity and better performance. However, federated mixedcriticality scheduling algorithm suffers resource waste as in federated scheduling, and almost half of processor resources can be wasted in extreme cases. In this paper, we address the problem and propose a novel semi-federated mixed-criticality algorithm (SFMC). SFMC combines semi-federated scheduling with mixedcriticality systems, whose original architecture is changed to a dual-hierarchical one. When analyzing the combined system, we first allocate finer-grained processor resources to each MC DAG task, then we prove the correctness of the SFMC algorithm in both normal and critical states. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on randomly generated independent DAG task sets based on OpenMP benchmarks. Experiment results present that our algorithm has better performance on schedulability than the federated mixed-criticality scheduling algorithm.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time scheduling theory is getting more and more attention, especially in the analysis of mixed-criticality and parallel task systems. Usually, researchers use mixed-criticality (MC) to describe a task which is safety-sensitive in realtime system. In the most common scenario, they consider two critical levels: high and low criticality. Generally, tasks of high criticality have higher priority when competing for computation resources and they must be finished before their deadlines. In some extreme cases, low-critical tasks may be discarded to ensure that high-critical tasks could finish before their deadlines. When checking the schedulability of a mixedcriticality system, independent conditions are performed in two states which are normal state and critical state. The system states determine which tasks in current system can be scheduled. The schedulability in critical state indicates the safety of MC system and the schedulability in normal state directly reflects the service quality offered to low-critical tasks.

Although multi-processors provide more computation resource to system, it is not a free lunch. Compared with single-processor platforms, modeling and analyzing are more complex and it is difficult to find the optimal schedulability test condition. Parallel real-time workload can be modeled by directed acyclic graph (DAG). Some classic DAG models have been proposed by researchers in recent years such as multi-DAG model [1] and conditional parallel task model [2].

The combination of mixed-criticality and parallel systems is drawing increasing attention, and many DAG mixed-criticality models have been proposed in recent years such as [3], [4]. In our work, we focus on federated mixed-ciricality (FMC-Li) [3], which is the state-of-art algorithm for MC DAG tasks. The algorithm is coarse-grained and the only parameter required are total workload and the longest path of a DAG task. The FMC-Li algorithm divides tasks into three types: HMH, HVH, and LH [3]. Each task is assigned separate processor resources, so it executes independently and does not compete with other tasks for resources. Compared to other MC DAG scheduling strategies, the FMC-Li algorithm has better performance and is more efficient.

However, the federated mixed-criticality scheduling suffers from resource waste. An MC DAG task may not fully consume processors allocated to it. For example, if a DAG task needs 2.1 processors, then with federated scheduling it will be allocated 2.1 = 3 processors and 90% of computation resource of one processor is wasted. In extreme cases, almost half of the total processor resource is wasted.

As far as we know this paper is the first work to integrate semi-federated scheduling with mixed-criticality system. We extend the techniques related to semi-federated by Xu et al [5] and propose Semi-federated Mixed-criticality algorithm (SFMC) to analyze the combined system. The SFMC completely overcomes the problem of resource waste mentioned above. In detail, we first assign precise processor resources to each mixed-criticality DAG task through the mapping algorithm, which reflects the minimum requirements of tasks for processor resources and differs in normal and critical states. And then we prove these mapping strategies.

The proposed SFMC integrates semi-federated scheduling with mixed-criticality systems and implements a hierarchical scheduling approach. This comlicated architecture causes difficulty to the schedulability analysis, which is the challenge fo this work.

Contribution: This paper proposes a semi-federated mixedcriticality algorithms to analyze parallel mixed-criticality systems. The semi-federated mixed-criticality algorithm is extended to calculate the response time of a DAG in both normal and critical states separately. In detail, we propose two mapping algorithms to determine the amount of processor resources required by each DAG task to ensure that these DAG tasks do not miss their deadlines. We generate large and random task sets as workload for our mixed-criticality system based on the real OpenMP [6] benchmarks. The experimental results show that performance with regard to schedulability of our algorithm is better than that of the federated mixed-criticality algorithm in parallel multi-processor platforms. The remaining of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II we present the model of MC DAG task and basic theories. In Section III, we present the details of SFMC algorithm. In Section IV we present evaluation of SFMC algorithm and comparison with the state-of-art. In Section V and Section VI, we present related work and conclusion.

div.head: A. MC task model
div.p: We consider a task set τ of n implicit-deadline mixedcriticality sporadic parallel tasks {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } on m identical processors with unit speed. Each task τ i is characterized by a triple (T i , G i ). T i is the minimum inter-arrival time between two consecutive jobs of task τ i . G i is a directed acyclic graph with G i = (V i , E i ). V i is the set of vertices in G i and E i is the set of directed edges connecting these vertices. Each vertex v ∈ V i is a code block which executes in a sequential order. A directed edge from s to v means that the vertex v can not start to execute before v has finished.

The criticality state of vertex v is represented by χ(v) ∈ {LO, HI}. When v is in state LO, its total worst-case execution time (WCET) is c N and its WCET is c O when it is in state HI. c N is obtained through a lot of repetitive independent experimental tests, and c O is generally estimated by theory. We use C N i , C O i to denote the sum of c N and c O for all v in V i respectively. We use L N i to denote the sum of c N of each vertex v along the longest chain of τ i and

The types of jobs that can be executed vary in different system states. In normal-state, lowcritical level tasks denoted as LO and high-critical level tasks denoted as HI are both allowed to utilize computing resource. In critical-state, only high-critical level tasks can be processed. div.head: B. Federated mixed-criticality scheduling
div.p: In federated mixed-criticality scheduling, tasks are divided to two types based on utilization: a task is called highutilization task if its utilization is larger than 1, else is called low-utilization task. For each high-utilization task, resource allocation is isolated and each task executes as if it was the only task. And low-utilization tasks are treated as traditional sequential real-time tasks and share the remaining processors. This strategy can not only minimize the use of processors, but also ensure that DAG tasks will not miss their deadline. We take HVH-task [3] as an example. div.head: C. Controling transition of MC states
div.p: One important concept in mixed-criticality system is virtual deadline. It was first proposed by EDF-VD [7] in single processor mixed-criticality systems. According to EDF-VD algorithm, each task is assigned a virtual deadline D which is usually less than D. The virtual deadline D is threshold point which controls system state transition. Once a task misses its virtual deadline D , the system enters a critical state and executes overload work of the task. If the value of D is too small, the system status will switch frequently. But if it is too large, there is no enough slack time to handle the overload work.

As shown in Figure 1, virtual deadline affects processor resource allocation in both two states. For a DAG task, the maximum workload that can be executed without deadline miss is fixed, which is C N in normal state and C O -C N in critical state. In other words, if the workload executed during the normal state is less than C N , then the task misses its virtual deadline and the system enters critical state. The smaller virtual deadline is, the easier a task misses its virtual deadline.

div.head: III. SEMI-FEDERATED MIXED-CRITICALITY ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section, we propose the semi-federated mixedciricality algorithm. First, we present whole architecture of our approach. Then, we describe each module of the SFMC algorithm in detail. Last, we prove the correctness of SFMC.

div.head: A. Architecture of SFMC
div.p: According to above analysis, the federated mixed-criticality algorithm uses a coarse-grained approach to allocate processors to DAG tasks. Each processor serves one DAG task in mixed-criticality system. Once a processor is occupied by a task, it will no longer provide service to other tasks regardless of the amount of remaining resource. In order to split processor resource based on different tasks' demand, we extend a lightweight virtualization technology and propose mixed-criticality container-task (MCCT). Now we directly show the architecture of SFMC algorithm with Figure 2. The architecture consists of two parts. One is how to calculate the mapping from MC DAG tasks to MCCTs. The other is to schedule MCCTs on physical processors and handle runtime state transitions. And in following section III-B and III-C, we will analyze and discuss these two parts of the architecture separately.

In order to better understand the SFMC algorithm, we first introduce the core component of the architecture which is named by container task [5]. A container task plays the role of processor resources interface and behaves as a dedicated processor with a slower speed. One task needs to be loaded into its container task first before it can be executed on a real processor. The load bound of a container task is denoted as δ. If the WCET of a task equals c when it executes on a unit speed processor, then its worst-case execution time on a processor with load bound δ is:

• normal-state (NS): This state is generally the initial state of a system. WCET of tasks in the state is obtained by a lot of engineering tests, so it can reflect the true system behavior of the DAG task. • critical-state (CS): Under certain special conditions a DAG task switches to this state which is more safe. The workload to be completed in this state is comparatively large and the amount is obtained from rigorous analysis and estimation. The following content is divided into two parts. First, we describe a mapping algorithm and prove it. Then we introduce that how MCCTs of a DAG task are filled with load on the condition that all of MCCTs in systems do not miss their deadlines.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we compare the schedulability performance between FMC-Li [3] and the SFMC algorithm we propose. We randomly generate a large number of DAG task sets and run them on our simulation platform. The simulation is running on a cloud platform with Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-26xx v4, cpu MHz 2394.

div.head: A. Generation of Task sets
div.p: The OpenMP [6] benchmark is often used by researchers to evaluate performance of parallel scheduling algorithms. These benchmark programs are based on C language and can not directly be executed on our simulation platform. So we use a tool ompTG [9] to transform these benchmarks to DAG collections. Table II is the baseline DAG collections for the task sets we generate.

Sine the baseline DAG does not have criticality attribution, we add a few parameters to it. b . In order to obtain more fair and accurate results, we generate more than 5000 task sets for each normalized utilization parameter.

div.head: B. Evaluation
div.p: Figure 3 compares the acceptance ratio of task sets scheduled with different algorithms: federated mixed-criticality algorithm [3] and semi-federated mixed-criticality algorithm. The X-axis indicates the sum of normalized utilization which is equal to maximum of (U N LO + U N HI , U O HI ) as formula 15.
div.formula: ⎧ ⎨ ⎩ U N LO + U N HI = u N i U O HI = u O i (15
div.p: Each task set contains low-criticality and high-criticality DAG tasks. The simulation system has two types of workload whose WCET are equal to C N LO and C N HI respectively. And only MC DAG tasks with C O HI can be executed in critical state. If one DAG task set meets its deadline in both two states, we say that it is schedulable. So we use the maximum of (U N LO + U N HI , U O HI ) to represent an MC DAG task set. From Figure 3(a), SFMC has much better schedulability performance than FMC-Li. When m = 8 and normalized utilization exceeds 0.7, DAG task sets can hardly be schedulable by FMC-Li. But the acceptance of our algorithm is still over 90 percent when normalized utilization is 0.9. The reason is that the SFMC algorithm uses more accurate calculation methods to allocate resources of processors, while FMC-Li algorithm [3] simply uses rounding up to calculate the number of processors needed by each DAG task set and allocates a complete processor to a DAG task set even if the fractional part of calculated number of required processors is very small. In Figure 3(b) and 3(c), we observe that the performance of both algorithms decreases. As the number of analog processors in our simulation system increases, the utilization of each DAG task increases. The increased demand for processors makes DAG task sets less likely to be scheduled before their deadlines. But our algorithm SFMC is still better than FMC-Li.

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: In this section we present some related work on real-time scheduling. Deng et al [14] encapsulated tasks requirements into Total Bandwidth Servers [15] and these servers are scheduled by host scheduler using EDF algorithm. Davis and Burns proposed a sporadic server to trace resource budgets of each task [16], and they analyzed schedulability of task sets when scheduled by a two-level EDF scheduling algorithm. Zhang and Burns extended the above work with a different real-time algorithm in two-level scheduling architecture [17]. Lu et al. implemented a hierarchical scheduling framework in a real platform which is named RT-XEN And they extended the framework with periodic server that is designed for fixed priority algorithm [18]. Govindan et al. proposed a scheduling algorithm that is communication-aware [19]. Recently, multiprocessor platform has drawn increasing attention and above work about hierarchical scheduling is extended to multiprocessor platforms [16], [20], [21] Parallel task models have been widely studied and promoted for a long time. Early researchers categorize parallel task models into the gang task model and the thread task model [22], [23]. Maia et al. analyzed both synchronous parallel task model and fork-join task model [24]. They treat a task as a few of sequential segments which are executed on multithreads at the same time. Fonseca et al. extended parallel task model to a more general model that is denoted as directed acyclic graph(DAG) [1]. There are three classic algorithm classifications for DAG scheduling that are decompositionbased scheduling [25], global scheduling [2] and federated scheduling [26]. For federated scheduling, Li et al. present a capacity augmentation bound of 2 for DAG tasks with implicit deadline [27]. Sanjoy applied federated scheduling to a new DAG task model with constrained-deadline and arbitrary-deadline [26].

Vestal et al. first proposed mixed-criticality system using a formal model [28]. Early researchers studied sequential mixed-criticality tasks on single processors [29], [30]. And Pathan et al. extended them to multi-processor platforms [31]. Liu et al proposed a decomposition-based algorithm that is mixed-ciricality synchronous task model [32]. Gu et al proposed a hierarchical component model with boundaries which are able to isolate low-criticality tasks from highcriticality tasks [29]. The model minimized the impact caused by high-criticality tasks on low-criticality tasks. Saravanan et al. explored the semi-partitioned scheduling model for dualcriticality system(SPMC) [33]. They proposed a server with budgets for each task and the server can run on different processors.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we propose the SFMC algorithm that is a dual-hierarchical scheduling approach. The SFMC algorithm consists of two parts which are the mapping algorithm and a conventional EDF algorithm. The mapping algorithm assigns precise processor resources to each MC DAG task. And in normal state and critical state, each task has two different resource mappings. We prove the correctness of these mapping strategies. And we propose a dispatcher algorithm to encapsulate each task into the fixed number MCCTs based on the above two mappings. According to the state of system changes, different sets of MCCTs can be allowed to run. The results of experiments show that our algorithm can still guarantee better schedulability performance when system load is high.

A mixed-ciricality task has a built-in property that is state transition. Most of approaches known are separate analysis tasks for each state of system. This may lead to waste of resources. By introducing a middle layer(virtualization technology), it is possible to solve this problem. In the next step, we will continue to study along this idea.
